name: Self-tanning drops

lead: Self-tanning drops are concentrated DHA that you mix into a moisturizer, lotion or face cream, so the number of drops sets how deep the colour gets. They are especially popular for the face, where a gradual, natural-looking tan is wanted.

Like other sunless tanners, DHA reacts with amino acids in the outer dead layer of skin to produce brown pigments. It is a cosmetic effect that does not stimulate melanin or provide UV protection. A 2026 systematic review of 16 studies and a 2023 safety review describe DHA as having a generally favourable topical safety profile.

paras: Users add drops to their regular face cream or body lotion and apply as normal, building colour over several days. More drops give a deeper result.

Mixing errors can give uneven colour, and drops can be too strong on the face. Keep DHA away from lips, eyes and mucous membranes; reviews note open questions about inhalation. A 2024 survey of 44 popular self-tanning products found contact allergens such as fragrances and propylene glycol were common. DHA gives minimal photoprotection, so sunscreen is still needed.

angle.text: Mixing DHA drops into your own face cream lets you build colour gradually and control the depth for a natural-looking face tan. The colouring comes from DHA reacting with the outer skin layer.

lead: Self-tanning drops are concentrated dihydroxyacetone (DHA) preparations that users mix into a moisturizer, lotion or face cream, so that the number of drops determines how deep the resulting colour is. They are especially discussed for face tanning, where a gradual, adjustable colour is wanted. [1]

The appearance payoff is a warmer, more even complexion without UV exposure: the colour develops over several hours, builds with repeat applications and fades over about a week as the skin exfoliates. Grokipedia describes drops as a way to get a gradual, customizable face tan without a separate product, and appearance forums discuss them for tanning the face. [1][2]

As with other sunless tanners, DHA reacts with amino acids in the outer dead layer of skin to produce brown pigments, a cosmetic effect that does not stimulate melanin or provide UV protection. [1][3][4] A 2026 systematic review of 16 studies and a 2023 safety review describe DHA as having a generally favourable topical safety profile, minimal photoprotection that is insufficient to replace sunscreen, and remaining questions about inhalation and effects on cells in vitro. A 2024 survey of 44 popular self-tanning products found that contact allergens such as fragrances and propylene glycol were common ingredients. [3][5][6]
infobox: Mixed into moisturizer or lotion; the drop count sets colour depth
Within hours, deepening over roughly 8 to 72 hours
About 3 to 10 days, fading as skin exfoliates
Cosmetic; DHA approved as a colour additive for external use only

paras: Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes drops as letting users customize tan intensity by adding more or fewer drops to a base product, producing a buildable colour. It lists drops among the forms of sunless tanner, alongside lotions, gels, mousses, sprays, creams and wipes, and gives DHA concentrations in sunless tanners of roughly 1 to 15 percent. [1] A 2018 review reports that commercial products commonly contain 3 to 5 percent DHA and that depth depends on concentration and the number of applications. [7]

Face-specific guidance that Grokipedia reports includes that facial skin is thinner and oilier than body skin, that facial formulas usually have lower DHA and are non-comedogenic, that product is kept away from the eyes, lips and nostrils, and that a patch test is advised. [1] Some products are tinted so that users can see where they have applied them, while clear formulas stain less but are harder to apply evenly. [1] Erythrulose, a slower-reacting sugar, is often blended with DHA for a more even result. [1][8]

Wikipedia reports that German scientists first recognized DHA as a skin-colouring agent in the 1920s, and that in the 1950s Eva Wittgenstein at the University of Cincinnati studied it as an oral treatment for children with glycogen storage disease; staff noticed that it browned skin where it spilled. [8] The first commercial DHA self-tanners, Man-Tan in 1959 and Coppertone's QT in 1960, gave orange-toned results that hurt the category's reputation. [9] The FDA added DHA to its approved cosmetic colour additives in the 1970s, and a 2018 review dates the first topical sunless tanning product marketed after the FDA colour additive review to 1977. [7][8]

Spray-tan booths from the late 1990s and reformulations broadened the market. [9] Grokipedia reports a 2025 Mintel figure that about 25 percent of US adults used self-tanners, up from 19 percent in 2022, with men and younger consumers a growing group. [1]

DHA is a simple sugar that darkens the stratum corneum through a non-enzymatic Maillard-type reaction with amino acids such as glycine, alanine, leucine and valine, producing brown pigments called melanoidins. Because it acts on surface cells, colour fades as these cells exfoliate. [7][8] A 2018 review reports that pigment appears within about an hour, peaks between 8 and 24 hours and lasts 5 to 7 days, with thinner facial skin needing reapplication sooner than thicker skin on the limbs. [7]

The pigmentation response to UV light, driven by melanocyte signalling through MC1R and MITF, is a separate biological pathway not engaged by DHA.  DHA has a very low SPF of about 3 according to Wikipedia, so it is not treated as a sunscreen. [8]

Drops are used in appearance communities for face tanning and for adjusting colour depth in a routine. Looksmax.org has threads on face tanning drops, on facial self-tanner and on the best self-tanner on the market, in which members compare products and ask how to avoid a patchy or orange face. [2][10][11] A looksmax.org thread describes the commonly reported failure mode: an application that missed the areas around the eyes, mouth and hairline, leaving a pale outline against an orange face, with replies suggesting abrasive scrubs or waiting for it to fade. [12]
A T Nation forum member described trying a self-tanner alongside body-hair removal and liking the result, one of several mentions of sunless tanning in physique-oriented communities. [13]

A 2023 survey analysis of the 2015 National Health Interview Survey found that 17.7 percent of US non-Hispanic white women aged 18 to 49 reported sunless tanning (lotion 15.3 percent, spray 6.8 percent), and 23.7 percent of sunless tanners also used indoor tanning. [14] A 2026 review of 37 top-selling sunless tanners found all contained DHA, erythrulose appeared in 38 percent, and only 3 percent included sunscreen. [14] A review of tanning biology notes that in some studies sunless tanner users wore hats or protective clothing less often and reported more sunburns, while sunscreen use did not differ. [4]
No clinical studies of drop formulations specifically were found. Studies of DHA generally include the following.

A 2026 systematic review in the Journal of Cutaneous Medicine and Surgery included 16 studies in humans and animal models. It reported that mouse data suggest minimal photoprotection insufficient to replace sunscreen and possible delay of UV-linked tumour development, that people with erythropoietic protoporphyria and vitiligo may benefit from DHA, and that no link had been established between DHA and clinically relevant vitamin deficiency or contact dermatitis, while concerns remain about free-radical formation and absorption. The authors noted that most studies were low quality with few participants and that some products exceeded the European Commission's permitted concentration. [3]

In a Thai study, 88.9 percent of 20 vitiligo patients reported moderate to marked satisfaction with 6 percent DHA cream as camouflage on exposed areas; a separate part of the study found higher DHA concentrations were needed to match darker skin. The study was small and partly retrospective. [15]

A 2023 uncontrolled case series of 19 people with erythropoietic protoporphyria estimated a protection factor of about 2 against UVA and visible light from DHA; 11 of 19 patients had a sustained good effect and kept using it through 2021. [14]

A cross-sectional review of 44 self-tanning products from 17 brands found an average of 11.86 contact allergens per product, most commonly propylene glycol, linalool, polysorbate, d-limonene, benzyl alcohol, tocopherol and fragrances. [6] Another review reports that allergic reactions to DHA itself are rare and are more often attributed to fragrances, preservatives and emulsifiers. [4]

The FDA regulates sunless tanners as cosmetics, permits DHA as a colour additive for external use only and advises avoiding ingestion, inhalation and contact with mucous membranes. [5][7] Reviews describe irritant and allergic contact dermatitis as reported reactions. [5] DHA does not offer meaningful UV protection, so sunscreen is still recommended by dermatology reviews. [3][5] Wikipedia gives DHA an SPF of about 3. [8]

A review of tanning biology notes laboratory work in which DHA caused oxidative stress and cell death in cultured cells at concentrations the authors describe as relevant to consumer use, mouse studies in which aerosolized DHA damaged the lungs, and in vitro estimates that a fraction of applied DHA reaches living epidermis. The authors call for human studies, and the 2023 safety review states that cytotoxicity requires concentrations far above those in tanning products. [4][5] Wikipedia also reports that DHA may increase free-radical damage from sunlight for about 24 hours at levels above 5 percent. [8]

Grokipedia reports that the EU and UK cap DHA at 10 percent in ready-to-use products, that topical DHA is generally considered low-risk in pregnancy because absorption is minimal, and that tanning pills containing canthaxanthin and unregulated melanotan peptides carry documented harms and are separate from topical tanners. [1] A 2026 review of tanning products describes rhabdomyolysis, renal infarction and priapism reported with unregulated melanotan use. [4] Dermatologists have also noted that DHA can cause follicular pigmentation that mimics lentigo maligna under dermoscopy, and advise patients to mention sunless tanner use. [4]

Related approaches to a tanned look include lotions, mousses and sprays that use the same active ingredient, wash-off bronzers, spray-tan booths and salons, and gradual tanning moisturizers. Looksmaxxing communities also discuss UV tanning, tanning beds and melanotan peptides, which have different mechanisms and risk profiles from topical DHA. [1][9]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and in physique forums, self-tanner and tanning drops are discussed as a quick way to add colour to the face, with threads about products and about fixing uneven application.[12][2][10][11]

claims.claim: Drops let you dial in a natural, buildable face tan.
A fake tan is safer than UV tanning.
Missed spots and streaks can be fixed by scrubbing or adding more.
Topical DHA is harmless to inhale or absorb.

timeline.event: German scientists recognize DHA as a skin-colouring agent. [8]
Eva Wittgenstein studies DHA in children with glycogen storage disease; skin browning is noticed where it spilled. [8][9]
Man-Tan becomes the first commercial DHA self-tanner. [9]
Coppertone launches QT; early products give orange-toned results. [8][9]
The FDA lists DHA among approved cosmetic colour additives. [8]
The first topical sunless tanning product after the FDA review is marketed, according to a 2018 review. [7]
Study of DHA as vitiligo camouflage published. [15]
Review of DHA properties and safety published; survey analysis reports 17.7 percent of US white women aged 18 to 49 used sunless tanners in 2015. [5][14]
Review finds contact allergens in all 44 popular self-tanning products examined. [6]
Systematic review of self-tanner (DHA) clinical use and safety published. [3]
